paras: The lynching of Thomas Kerr was the hanging of Thomas P. Kerr from a sycamore tree at the Pioneer mining camp in Arizona Territory early on December 26, 1882, by men of the camp who had tried him before their own jury of twelve. Kerr had been accused of shooting a man named as William Hartley or William Hartnett in a Pioneer saloon hours before. A Tucson Citizen dispatch carried the story across the country, and a coroner's jury later found that Kerr died by hanging by unknown parties.

Globe's Arizona Silver Belt described Kerr as long regarded there as a dangerous man, reported to have fled Montana and to have killed a man at San Luis Obispo, California. The Yuma Arizona Sentinel said he had killed a man it called Mat Bludsoe, while the Sacramento version of the wire named a Hank Bludsee of Tucson among the men Kerr confessed to killing. None of the papers gives the race of Kerr or of the man he was accused of killing.

According to the wire, Hartley stepped up to the bar for a drink when Kerr, "without provocation," knocked him down and, saying "Young fellow, now I've got you," shot him dead. The Sacramento Record-Union's fuller text said Kerr fired five shots during a scuffle on the floor, put out the lights and struck the dead man with his pistol seven times. The Silver Belt instead traced the killing to words between the two men about a horse on the night of the 25th, after which Kerr fired four shots and handed his revolver and knife to Charles Wood.

Kerr was disarmed and held in a back room while miners and men of the camp called a jury of twelve, which found him "guilty of murder" and ordered him hanged at once. Given an hour, he wrote to his mother at Lexington, Illinois, asking that his effects go to her, and called for drinks. At about 1 a.m. he was pinioned, given a whiskey at Nicholson's bar and taken to a sycamore near the Pioneer blacksmith shop. There, by the wire's account, he confessed killing several men, was drawn up once and let down, took off his boots so as not to die with them on, and was hanged; his body was cut down in the morning.

A coroner's jury empaneled by Judge George A. Allen returned a verdict that Kerr "came to his death by hanging by unknown parties." No report of arrests or prosecution of the lynchers appears in the coverage. From Kerr's hometown, an Inter Ocean special said his mother and sisters were crushed, that he "was not a desperado," and that people there refused to believe he killed Hartley without grave provocation.

The Tucson Citizen's Globe dispatch reached San Francisco on December 26 and ran the next day in the New-York Tribune as "A Murderer Lynched" and in the Sacramento Record-Union as "Murder and Lynching." Nevada papers printed it on December 28, the Eureka Sentinel naming the dead man "William Hardy" and the Carson City Morning Appeal placing it under the deck "Judicious Lynching in Arizona." Other dailies, such as the Knoxville Daily Chronicle, used headlines on Kerr's coolness and his boots, and crime columns compressed it to a line about "a lynchers' jury of 12."

The local Silver Belt, a weekly published on December 30, was openly approving, headlining "A Cruel Murder And a Just Retribution" and calling the hanging "merited retribution." It explained that the citizens feared a court would acquit Kerr, as had happened in two other murder trials in the county, and linked the hanging to the hanging of two accused murderers at Globe the previous August. The Sacramento text added that popular opinion in Globe held Kerr "should have been hanged long ago," while the Ottawa Free Trader in Illinois retold the affair with sarcasm, calling the jurors "business men of the town." No Black-press coverage of the episode was found.

The dead man's name varied between Hartley in the wire, Hardy and Harthy in Nevada reprints, Jno. Hartley in the Yuma paper and Hartnett in the Globe weekly, the local paper being the most considered source. The wire's claim that Kerr acted without provocation was contradicted by the Silver Belt's quarrel and scuffle and doubted by his hometown, and the Silver Belt itself noted "many conflicting statements of the affair."

bases: Men of the Pioneer camp held their own jury of twelve over Thomas Kerr after a saloon killing and hanged him from a sycamore tree; a coroner's jury found he died by hanging by unknown parties (A2, A14, A15).

Kerr was hanged by 'citizens' after an informal trial before a jury of twelve that had no lawful authority, and the coroner attributed the death to unknown parties (A4, A14, A15). The pretext was punishment for the killing of Hartley/Hartnett (A2, A14).

The Tucson Citizen wire carried in California, Nevada and Eastern papers and the independent local account in Globe's Arizona Silver Belt agree on the saloon killing, the jury of twelve and the hanging from a sycamore, and a coroner's verdict confirms the death by hanging (A2, A4, A14, A15).

framing.detail: The Globe Silver Belt headlined 'A Cruel Murder And a Just Retribution' and 'Thomas P. Kerr's Sixth Victim', called the hanging 'merited retribution' and linked it to the August hanging of two other accused murderers.
The Carson City Morning Appeal put the wire under the deck 'Judicious Lynching in Arizona'.
Eastern and Western dailies ran the Tucson Citizen wire as 'A Murderer Lynched' or 'A Murderer Taking Lynching Cooly', dwelling on Kerr's coolness and the boots.
The Ottawa Free Trader retold the story sardonically, calling Kerr 'a typical Arizonian' and the jurors 'business men of the town'.
